paragraphs: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning evaluates the distribution of cumulative rewards rather than focusing only on their average. This paper studies optimized certainty equivalents, a family covering objectives such as conditional value-at-risk, entropic risk, and mean-variance preferences. Its target is a policy that can use the history of an interaction when choosing actions.

The authors develop two overarching algorithms, one using optimism and another using policy gradients. Both convert the risk-sensitive problem into an augmented Markov decision process where existing risk-neutral learning algorithms can be applied. This reduction matters because it lets the researchers reuse established algorithms and theoretical tools instead of developing a separate learning theory for each risk objective.

The optimism-based analysis extends previous conditional value-at-risk results and supplies the first risk-sensitive bounds for exogenous block MDPs. For the gradient-based method, monotone improvement and global convergence require a discrete reward assumption. A proof-of-concept experiment also shows the algorithms learning an optimal history-dependent policy in a constructed environment where every Markovian policy provably fails, illustrating why memory can matter for these objectives.
icml-2025-a-reductions-approach-to-risk-.tldr: Two reductions let risk-sensitive reinforcement learning reuse risk-neutral algorithms while supporting policies that depend on interaction history.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can struggle when a web task requires a long sequence of coordinated actions. Agent Workflow Memory addresses this by extracting reusable routines from previous experiences and selectively supplying those routines during later tasks. The central idea is to turn experience into procedural guidance that can help an agent organize future actions.

The method supports two ways of building this memory. In the offline setting, workflows are derived from training examples before deployment. In the online setting, they are induced from test queries as the agent works. This flexibility makes workflow reuse applicable both when relevant examples already exist and when useful routines must emerge during ongoing interaction.

Experiments use Mind2Web and WebArena, together covering more than 1,000 tasks across over 200 domains. The reported relative success-rate improvements are 24.6% and 51.1%, respectively, and successful WebArena tasks require fewer steps. Online workflow memory also exceeds baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points across evaluations with widening task-distribution gaps. These results support reusable workflows as a practical aid to both task completion and generalization.
icml-2025-agent-workflow-memory-422ab109.tldr: Agent Workflow Memory extracts reusable routines from experience to improve web agents’ success, efficiency, and generalization.

paragraphs: This paper develops a transformer architecture from an explicit view of representation learning: noisy token representations should be compressed toward a mixture of low-dimensional subspaces. Under this view, learning useful representations means progressively removing noise while retaining the structure described by those subspaces. The authors use this proposed objective to motivate the network’s components.

The associated denoising operation takes the form of multi-head subspace self-attention. Repeating that operation and expressing the iterations as network layers produces a compact architecture containing only self-attention and skip connections. Each layer therefore has an interpretable role as a denoising step, connecting the architecture directly to the mathematical process from which it was derived.

The authors show that signal-to-noise ratio improves at a linear rate with network depth in their analysis. Experiments on vision and language tasks find performance close to standard transformer architectures including GPT-2 and CRATE. The findings suggest that this simpler, mathematically motivated architecture can retain substantial practical capability, while the claim of comparable performance remains an empirical result from the reported tasks.
icml-2025-attention-only-transformers-vi.tldr: Unrolling a subspace-denoising process yields an interpretable attention-only transformer with performance close to standard architectures in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Identifying a relationship between variables does not by itself establish which variable causes the other. This paper studies how to choose experimental interventions that help determine that direction. It frames the decision as hypothesis testing, emphasizing the strength of evidence for competing explanations rather than only the amount of information an intervention is expected to provide.

The proposed strategy uses Bayes factors to compare support for one hypothesis against another. It also plans intervention values across multiple steps, balancing evidence that can be gained immediately against evidence obtainable through future experiments. This makes intervention selection a sequential planning problem, with choices evaluated partly through their consequences for later testing.

By analyzing this objective, the authors derive a dynamic programming algorithm that reduces its computational complexity from non-polynomial to polynomial. Experiments cover two-variable systems, tree-structured graphs, and an embodied AI environment. The results support the framework’s effectiveness for identifying causal direction and show its potential extension beyond two-variable problems. The contribution combines an evidence-focused experimental objective with a more tractable way to plan intervention sequences.
icml-2025-bayesian-active-learning-for-b.tldr: A Bayes-factor objective and dynamic programming guide sequential interventions toward stronger evidence about causal direction.

paragraphs: Query access to a deployed graph neural network can allow another model to learn from its outputs. This creates a model-extraction vulnerability, but selective querying also has legitimate uses when obtaining labels is expensive. CEGA examines both perspectives, focusing on how to acquire useful supervision with a tightly restricted query budget.

The method targets a setting where bulk queries are forbidden and only a small initial collection of nodes is available. It repeatedly updates its node-selection strategy over successive learning cycles, using feedback from earlier queries to improve later choices. The purpose is to spend limited queries on informative nodes rather than treating every available node as equally valuable.

Benchmark experiments report better accuracy, fidelity, and F1 scores than comparable baselines under strict query-size constraints. Fidelity captures the replication goal, while predictive performance also matters for authorized model acquisition. The findings therefore have two implications: deployed graph models can remain vulnerable even with constrained access, and adaptive node selection can help researchers build useful models when supervision is costly or scarce.
icml-2025-cega-a-cost-effective-approach.tldr: CEGA adapts node queries using past feedback to improve graph-model extraction and authorized acquisition under tight query constraints.

paragraphs: Learning continuously from images with multiple labels creates overlapping difficulties: earlier knowledge can be forgotten, some labels may be missing, and class frequencies can be uneven. This paper focuses on the image regions associated with individual labels. Such regions offer more specific learning signals, but identifying them is difficult when supervision arrives incrementally and is incomplete.

The authors first use structural information in the input to assess how well different pretrained models can already localize relevant regions. Their CUTER strategy then identifies and strengthens label-specific regions, cuts them out, and uses them for experience replay. Replaying these targeted pieces gives the learner finer-grained supervision than relying only on the original multi-label image context.

The proposed strategy is designed to address forgetting, missing labels, and class imbalance together. It is also presented as complementary to existing approaches, allowing region-focused replay to be integrated with other techniques. Experiments on multiple multi-label image benchmarks report superior performance. The findings support label-specific localization and replay as a useful shared mechanism for several difficulties that arise in continual learning.
icml-2025-cut-out-and-replay-a-simple-ye.tldr: CUTER replays label-specific image regions to help continual learners handle forgetting, missing labels, and class imbalance together.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality samples, but repeatedly evaluating their networks makes sampling costly. Numerical solvers reduce that cost by using fewer steps. This paper examines a common design choice in advanced solvers: building their updates around time-based Lagrange interpolation, inherited from Adams-like multistep numerical methods.

The authors show that this interpolation choice is suboptimal for diffusion models and identify a compact search space involving both sampling times and solver coefficients. They then introduce a differentiable search algorithm to choose those quantities. The approach makes the numerical update rule itself something that can be optimized, rather than accepting a conventional interpolation rule as fixed.

With 10 sampling steps on ImageNet at 256 by 256 resolution, the searched solvers achieve FID scores of 2.40 for SiT-XL/2, 2.35 for FlowDCN-XL/2, and 2.33 for DiT-XL/2. The paper reports substantial improvements over traditional solvers and applicability across architectures, resolutions, and model sizes. These findings support solver design as an effective route to improving generation quality when the sampling budget is small.
icml-2025-differentiable-solver-search-f.tldr: Differentiable search jointly optimizes sampling times and solver coefficients to improve diffusion generation with few sampling steps.

paragraphs: Fast diffusion sampling often requires a tradeoff between generation quality and computational cost. Distillation can help, but may introduce substantial training and parameter-storage overhead. This paper proposes PCA-based Adaptive Search, or PAS, which improves existing numerical solvers through a very small learned correction rather than a large additional model.

PAS first uses principal component analysis to find a few basis vectors describing the high-dimensional sampling space. It then learns coordinates within that smaller space to adjust the sampling direction. An adaptive search procedure builds on the observed S-shaped pattern of cumulative truncation error, improving sampling efficiency while reducing the stored correction parameters to approximately ten.

The reported experiments show that PAS improves existing fast solvers with little additional cost. In one CIFAR10 result, it changes DDIM’s FID from 15.69 to 4.37 at 10 function evaluations, using 12 parameters and less than a minute of training on one A100 GPU. This example illustrates how a low-dimensional correction can produce a substantial quality gain without the training and storage demands associated with larger sampling adaptations.
icml-2025-diffusion-sampling-correction-.tldr: PAS improves fast diffusion solvers by learning low-dimensional sampling corrections with approximately ten stored parameters.

paragraphs: Differentiable control lets a controller participate in learning by passing gradients to the quantities that determine its behavior. The iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator is a candidate for this role, but differentiating through many optimization iterations can be expensive. DiLQR makes this controller usable as a trainable module, either by itself or inside a larger neural network.

Its central contribution is an analytical gradient obtained through implicit differentiation. The method provides an accurate gradient while keeping the backward computation cost constant with respect to the number of solver iterations. This addresses the expense of differentiating through the iterative computation, without claiming that cost is independent of every aspect of the control problem.

On imitation-learning control benchmarks, the analytical method runs 21 to 128 times faster than automatic differentiation. The paper also reports stronger learning performance than traditional neural policies and better model loss than differentiable controllers without exact analytical gradients. Integration into a larger network receiving visual inputs demonstrates that the controller can support high-dimensional, end-to-end learning as well as the benchmark control tasks.
icml-2025-dilqr-differentiable-iterative.tldr: DiLQR uses analytical implicit gradients to make iterative control substantially faster to differentiate and usable in end-to-end learning.

paragraphs: A foundation model such as CLIP can struggle when new images differ substantially from its training data. Fine-tuning can help, but collecting all relevant data centrally may be infeasible because of privacy concerns. This paper addresses adaptation across separate data holders while also seeking good performance on domains outside those used for adaptation.

The proposed Federated Adapter Generalization method, FedAG, uses multiple fine-grained adapters in a cross-silo federated setting. These adapters capture domain-specific knowledge through parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Quality-aware mutual learning operates within domains, while attention-regularized learning connects domains. Together, these mechanisms are intended to integrate specialized knowledge while supporting broader generalization.

Experiments adapt CLIP on ImageCLEF-DA, Office-Home, and DomainNet, three datasets involving domain shifts. The authors report superior performance both within the participating domains and outside them. These findings support the idea that federated adaptation can do more than specialize a model to each data source: carefully coordinating domain-specific adapters can also improve its ability to handle unfamiliar domains in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-enhancing-foundation-models-wi.tldr: FedAG coordinates domain-specific adapters across federated data holders to improve CLIP’s in-domain and out-of-domain performance.

paragraphs: Synthetic code training data often starts from existing snippets, which can constrain the variety and complexity of the examples produced. EpiCoder introduces a synthesis framework organized around hierarchical code features instead. The goal is to generate examples from a richer description of programming patterns and relationships, giving more direct control over the resulting training material.

The framework constructs a feature tree from raw data and repeatedly refines it to expand the number and diversity of features represented. Sampling subtrees with different depths and breadths controls code complexity. This supports examples ranging from individual function operations to scenarios involving multiple files, connecting the organization of the feature tree to the scope of the generated code.

The authors fine-tune widely used base models on the synthesized data to produce the EpiCoder series. They report state-of-the-art results across multiple function-level and file-level benchmarks. Their experiments also indicate potential for generating repository-level code data. That repository-scale finding is presented as promising evidence, while the stated benchmark achievements concern function-level and file-level performance.
icml-2025-epicoder-encompassing-diversit.tldr: EpiCoder synthesizes code from hierarchical feature trees, controlling example complexity and improving function-level and file-level code-generation results.

paragraphs: Federated learning has two distinct generalization challenges. A model must perform well on new examples from clients that participated in training, and it must also transfer to clients that did not participate. This paper analyzes both the out-of-sample gap and the participation gap within a single information-theoretic framework.

The authors extend conditional mutual information analysis by introducing a superclient construction that accommodates variation at the client level. They derive several bounds, including ones showing how privacy constraints can imply generalization guarantees. The resulting analysis links properties of a federated learning procedure to both levels of generalization rather than treating unseen examples as the only source of uncertainty.

Their fast-rate evaluated bounds recover the best-known convergence rate when empirical risk is small. Further improvements in dependence on the number of participating clients apply to particular aggregation strategies and structured loss functions. Empirical evaluations find that the evaluated bounds are non-vacuous and track the algorithms’ generalization behavior. These results make the theory informative in the tested settings while retaining the stated conditions behind its sharper guarantees.
icml-2025-generalization-in-federated-le.tldr: A conditional mutual information framework bounds federated learning’s generalization to both unseen examples and non-participating clients.

paragraphs: Graphs whose nodes contain text offer a way to apply language models when labeled graph data is scarce. However, large neighborhoods can exceed a model’s context capacity, and graph embeddings may not align well with its token representations. This paper develops LLM-BP around two principles intended to improve generalization across such graphs.

The first principle aligns text attributes through task-adaptive embeddings. Language-model encoders and task-aware prompts produce representations suited to the inference task. The second principle concerns how information moves across graph connections: LLM-BP uses belief propagation with parameters estimated by a language model and adapted across graphs. This separates textual representation from the mechanism that combines graph information.

Across 11 real-world text-attributed graph benchmarks, the authors report a significant advantage over existing methods. They attribute an 8.10% improvement to task-conditional embeddings and a further 1.71% gain to adaptive aggregation. The findings suggest that both parts matter: adapting how node text is represented and adapting how neighboring information is combined each contribute to the reported generalization performance.
icml-2025-generalization-principles-for-.tldr: LLM-BP combines task-adaptive text embeddings with language-model-guided belief propagation to improve inference on text-attributed graphs.

paragraphs: Curiosity-based reinforcement learning encourages an agent to explore, which can help in environments where useful rewards are difficult to discover. Yet these methods often need extensive hyperparameter tuning for each environment. This paper investigates that sensitivity through agent behavior and identifies difficulties in both choosing an appropriate hyperparameter and optimizing the resulting learning process.

The proposed method, Hyper, regulates exploration visitation and decouples exploitation to stabilize training. These mechanisms address how the agent explores and how it learns to take advantage of rewards. The aim is to substantially reduce the tuning problem, making curiosity-driven exploration more robust across environments rather than depending as heavily on environment-specific adjustments.

The authors provide a theoretical efficiency result in a function-approximation setting and report empirical performance and robustness across multiple environments. Together, these findings support Hyper as a way to reduce a practical obstacle to using curiosity-based methods. The claim is that the method mitigates hyperparameter sensitivity and optimization instability; the abstract does not frame it as eliminating every tuning decision.
icml-2025-hyper-hyperparameter-robust-ef.tldr: Hyper regulates exploration and separates exploitation to reduce hyperparameter sensitivity and stabilize curiosity-based reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Fine-grained image retrieval must distinguish categories that can look almost identical while searching efficiently. Hashing addresses efficiency by representing images with short binary codes. This paper aims to make those codes more informative and interpretable by connecting individual bits to specific visual attributes rather than leaving their meaning implicit.

The method uses learnable queries to capture subtle attribute-level information during hash-code learning. It also adds an auxiliary branch that models higher-order interactions among attributes. That branch helps with the difficult optimization associated with short codes, where a limited number of bits must preserve the distinctions needed for accurate retrieval.

Experiments on benchmark datasets report attribute-aware codes and consistently better retrieval accuracy and robustness than state-of-the-art alternatives, particularly when codes contain few bits. The findings suggest that explicitly organizing the representation around attributes can improve both its usefulness and its interpretability. The auxiliary interaction modeling further supports compact codes by helping represent relationships among visual attributes within the constrained binary representation.
icml-2025-learning-attribute-aware-hash-.tldr: Learnable attribute queries and an auxiliary interaction model improve compact image-retrieval hash codes, especially at low bit counts.

paragraphs: Formal theorem proving requires a proposed proof to satisfy a computer-verifiable language such as Lean4. Generating an entire proof and diagnosing errors place different demands on a language model. MA-LoT addresses the difficulty of balancing these activities by using model collaboration to separate whole-proof generation from error analysis and correction.

The framework organizes extended reasoning around structured interaction between language models and the Lean4 verifier. It also introduces a training-and-inference pipeline called LoT-Transfer Learning, intended to give models long-chain reasoning capabilities without special data annotation. The contribution therefore includes both a collaborative proving process and a way to prepare models for that process.

On the Lean4 version of MiniF2F-Test, MA-LoT achieves 61.07% accuracy. The stated comparisons are 33.61% for DeepSeek-V3, 50.70% for InternLM-Step-Prover’s single-model tree search, and 55.33% for Godel-Prover’s whole-proof generation. These results support combining extended reasoning, distinct model roles, and formal feedback for this benchmark. The paper also presents the combination of long reasoning and verification as a promising direction for more insightful proof generation.
icml-2025-ma-lot-model-collaboration-lea.tldr: MA-LoT coordinates proof generation and correction through language-model collaboration and Lean4 verification, reaching 61.07% on MiniF2F-Test.

paragraphs: Accurate numerical flow simulation can be expensive because it requires fine spatial grids and small time steps. Learned simulators can accelerate computation but may struggle with generalization and accumulating prediction errors. MultiPDENet combines numerical-method structure with learning to support faster simulation while retaining explicit guidance from the governing partial differential equations.

A convolutional filter shaped like a finite-difference stencil learns a small number of parameters to estimate spatial derivatives on a coarse grid. Its training minimizes the equation residual. A Physics Block then embeds the PDE structure and advances predictions using a fourth-order Runge-Kutta integrator at a fine time scale. At a coarser time scale, another neural component corrects prediction error.

This multiscale design targets the accumulation of errors during long simulations. Experiments across PDE systems, including Navier-Stokes equations, report accurate long-term dynamics even with small, incomplete, or downsampled training data. The authors also report state-of-the-art performance against neural baselines and clear acceleration over classical numerical methods. The findings support combining physically structured updates with learned corrections for the evaluated flow problems.
icml-2025-multipdenet-pde-embedded-learn.tldr: MultiPDENet combines PDE-guided numerical updates with learned corrections at multiple time scales for faster, accurate long-term flow simulation.

paragraphs: Selecting instruction-tuning examples by how much they reduce next-token prediction loss may not select the examples that most improve a target task. For instance, better token prediction and a higher code pass rate are different objectives. NICE addresses this mismatch by basing data selection on the task’s evaluation metric, even when that metric is not differentiable.

The method uses policy gradients to estimate which training examples will help improve measured performance. This provides a way to guide selection using the desired outcome instead of relying on validation loss as a proxy. NICE can also select data without ground-truth responses when the evaluation metric itself does not need them, such as scores supplied by a reward model.

Experiments report improvements over selection baselines based on next-token prediction loss across varied, realistic scenarios. Models trained on NICE-selected subsets also often outperform models trained on the full dataset. These findings support task-aligned curation: additional examples are not always as helpful as a smaller collection chosen for its estimated effect on the performance measure that matters.
icml-2025-nice-data-selection-for-instru.tldr: NICE uses policy-gradient influence estimates to select instruction-tuning data for non-differentiable task metrics rather than token-prediction loss.

paragraphs: Natural spoken dialogue depends on more than generating a suitable verbal response. A model must also capture conversational dynamics, including when speakers take turns. This paper studies dual-channel speech data, which preserves the structure of a conversation across two channels, as a resource for learning more fluid spoken interactions.

The authors introduce Next-Token-Pair Prediction, or NTPP, as a generative modeling approach for speaker-independent dual-channel dialogue. It uses a decoder-only architecture and makes paired-token prediction central to learning from the two channels. The approach is intended to make fuller use of the conversational structure already present in dual-channel recordings.

On standard benchmarks, NTPP improves turn-taking prediction, response coherence, and naturalness relative to existing approaches. It also achieves substantially lower inference latency in the reported comparisons. These findings connect the modeling choice to both conversational behavior and practical response speed: exploiting the two-channel structure helps the model learn how dialogue unfolds while supporting the low delays needed for real-time spoken interaction.
icml-2025-ntpp-generative-speech-languag.tldr: NTPP learns dual-channel spoken dialogue through paired-token prediction, improving conversational behavior and reducing inference latency in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Generative image steganography conceals a secret image inside another generated image. Existing diffusion-based approaches can leave the visible image looking unnatural or too similar to the secret, increasing detection risk. The paper also identifies degraded secret-image recovery and security problems when descriptive text prompts serve as the keys used in the process.

SSHR combines reference images with adaptive keys to guide generation and recovery. Reference-based guidance aims to make the visible images more natural and the hidden content less perceptible. The framework also introduces an Exact Reveal Process to improve reconstruction, addressing problems associated with inconsistent intermediate states between diffusion sampling and inversion.

Its symmetric keys depend on both the reference and secret images, providing an alternative to using descriptive prompts as keys. Experiments report better recovery quality and secret-image security than existing methods. The contribution brings together control of the visible image, improved recovery of the hidden image, and a revised key mechanism. The reported security advantage is comparative experimental evidence, rather than a claim that concealment is impossible to detect.
icml-2025-sshr-more-secure-generative-st.tldr: SSHR combines reference-image guidance, adaptive symmetric keys, and an improved reveal process to strengthen image concealment and recovery.

paragraphs: Contrast-enhanced MRI workflows often need images acquired before contrast administration for comparison and quantitative analysis. Those pre-contrast images may be absent, degraded, or difficult to align with later scans. This paper addresses that gap by synthesizing pre-contrast images directly from post-contrast MRI, aiming to supply information needed by workflows that use both image types.

The proposed learning framework proceeds in stages and incorporates physical grounding together with a hyperintensity prior. These are the stated foundations of its synthesis approach. Producing the missing image from an existing post-contrast scan could reduce the need for additional imaging sessions and the associated costs and patient burdens.

The authors evaluate the model across datasets, clinical sites, anatomies, and downstream tasks, reporting robustness and clinical applicability. They describe it, to their knowledge, as the first pre-contrast synthesis model whose outputs may be used interchangeably with standard-of-care pre-contrast images. That wording expresses a possibility supported by their evaluations, rather than establishing unconditional equivalence. The stated findings position the method as a potentially useful addition to contrast-enhanced MRI workflows.
icml-2025-staged-and-physics-grounded-le.tldr: A staged, physics-grounded model synthesizes pre-contrast MRI from post-contrast scans, with evaluations supporting potential clinical use.

paragraphs: Rectified-flow models can generate strong images and videos, but errors when inverting existing content can reduce their usefulness for editing. This paper targets the numerical errors involved in solving the underlying ordinary differential equation. Its RF-Solver is a training-free sampler designed to make inversion more precise.

The authors derive an exact formulation of the rectified-flow equation and use a high-order Taylor expansion to approximate its nonlinear components. This improves the precision of the numerical solution at each time step. Building on the solver, RF-Edit transfers self-attention features from inversion into editing, helping preserve the source image’s or video’s structure while making the requested changes.

The approach is presented as compatible with pretrained rectified-flow models for both image and video tasks, without additional training or optimization. Experiments across generation, inversion, and editing report superior performance and versatility. The two contributions address connected problems: more accurate numerical inversion provides a stronger basis for editing, and feature sharing helps carry structural information from the original content into the edited result.
icml-2025-taming-rectified-flow-for-inve.tldr: RF-Solver improves rectified-flow inversion without training, while RF-Edit reuses inversion features to preserve structure during image and video editing.

paragraphs: Sound carries information about physical conditions, including motion, propagation paths, and spatial relationships. ACORN aims to teach language models to interpret such information, focusing on phenomena including the Doppler effect and multipath effects. The paper treats audio as a source of evidence about the physical world, extending beyond recognition of spoken content.

To address scarce training data, the authors create a physics-based simulator that combines real sound sources with controlled physical channels. They use it to construct AQA-PHY, an audio question-answering dataset. The framework also introduces an audio encoder that processes both magnitude and phase information, then connects that encoder to existing language models.

The authors report reasonable results on simulated and real-world tasks involving line-of-sight detection, Doppler-effect estimation, and direction-of-arrival estimation. These findings provide evidence that the framework can learn useful physical cues from sound in the studied settings. The contribution combines controlled data generation with an audio representation designed to retain physical information, offering a route toward broader physical awareness without claiming that the problem is solved.
icml-2025-teaching-physical-awareness-to.tldr: ACORN combines simulated physical acoustics and magnitude-and-phase audio encoding to teach language models to infer physical properties from sound.

paragraphs: Text placed inside an image can interfere with a vision-language model’s predictions, but the reason for that interference is unclear. This paper asks whether the model is responding to word meaning or to visual appearance. It introduces the ToT dataset to separate these possibilities through controlled comparisons of words.

The dataset pairs synonyms, which share meaning but look different, and paronyms, which look similar but differ in meaning. The authors then analyze intrinsic dimension across model layers to study how representations change. Early layers show competing dynamics between spelling-related appearance and semantics. Later increases in semantic accuracy accompany lower intrinsic dimension, but much of that improvement is attributed to resolving visual differences between words.

Clear semantic differentiation appears only in the final block in the reported analysis. This challenges the assumption that understanding word meaning develops steadily throughout the network. The findings suggest that visual texture and orthographic disambiguation play a substantial role in how the studied models process text inside images, helping explain why apparent reading ability does not necessarily reflect semantic processing at every layer.
icml-2025-textural-or-textual-how-vision.tldr: Controlled word-pair experiments suggest that visual form drives much of image-text processing, with clear semantic differentiation emerging only in the final block.

paragraphs: Planning a sequence of interventions requires deciding how to guide a changing system toward a desired outcome. This paper formalizes that problem as counterfactual target achievement, motivated by personalized healthcare. It highlights a difficulty with directly using counterfactual prediction methods: errors can compound across a sequence because the alternative outcomes being considered are not observed.

Variational Counterfactual Intervention Planning, or VCIP, changes the modeling objective to the conditional likelihood of reaching the target outcome. It implements this formulation through variational inference. The method also uses the g-formula to connect interventional and observational log-likelihoods, providing the basis for training the planner from observational data.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report significantly higher target-achievement accuracy than existing methods. The result supports organizing the learning problem around whether an intervention sequence reaches its goal. This focus is directly aligned with the planning task described in the paper: the desired output is a sequence that guides the system toward a target, and the reported evaluation measures success at achieving that target.
icml-2025-variational-counterfactual-int.tldr: VCIP learns intervention plans from observational data by modeling the likelihood of reaching a target outcome through variational inference.
